articles.full_article_text: Databricks is riding high. Fresh off the back of announcing Genie One at its recent DATA + AI SUMMIT in San Francisco, the cloud-based data intelligence and AI platform has confirmed strategic funding that takes its valuation to an eye-watering US$188bn. The company calls Genie One "the next evolution of Genie," helping marketing, finance, sales and more automate and orchestrate their work grounded in real business data. Rich Radley, its EMEA VP of Field Engineering, is well placed to lift the lid on Genie One, not to mention Databricks's various innovation in the field of AI. In his role, Rich works with organisations across Europe to help them turn advances in data and AI into measurable business outcomes. Before joining Databricks, he spent almost a decade at Google, helping build Google Cloud's business across the UK and Ireland and supporting organisations as they modernised their technology and data strategies. “What really drew me to Databricks was the opportunity ahead,” Rich explains. “It felt like the company was at a real turning point, with AI changing not only the technology organisations use, but also the conversations they're having in the boardroom. That's something I find really exciting. “My role is about helping customers connect the technology with the business outcome, while supporting my team to have more strategic conversations that show how data and AI can create long-term value.” “ Given the pace of modern businesses, this empowers decision makers like never before and acts as a key strategic differentiator. ” Rich Radley Rich Radley, EMEA VP of Field Engineering How Genie One is different from other AI assistants Rich argues that we've reached a point where the AI models themselves are incredibly capable. He says the real challenge now is giving them enough understanding of a business to produce outputs that people can genuinely rely on. “Without that,” he says, "even the most advanced assistants can deliver responses that sound plausible but miss the nuances of how an organisation actually operates.” "Genie One addresses this issue directly by being powered by Genie Ontology, a live context layer that continuously learns from your organisation’s data, metrics, systems and knowledge. Rather than simply interpreting prompts or individual documents, it understands the relationships between them, enabling it to deliver responses that reflect how the business actually works.” Rich explains that, with it, employees can spend less time searching for information or validating AI outputs, and more time making decisions and taking action. “More importantly,” he goes on, "it opens up data and AI to far more people across the organisation, removing some of the traditional dependency on technical teams while still operating within the right governance and security guardrails. “That's where I think businesses will see the biggest impact." “ Businesses can empower more people to work with data while maintaining the controls, security and oversight needed to scale AI responsibly. That's what true democratisation looks like. ” Rich Radley EMEA VP of Field Engineering Interesting use cases from non-technical teams Rich argues that the real power of Genie One is "putting trusted data into the hands of those that need it in seconds, fundamentally changing the speed at which decisions are made". He continues: "Imagine a sales leader meeting with the CEO. Instead of saying they'll come back with the numbers, they can instantly access the latest data insights on their mobile device, analyse information in real time, ask follow-up questions and respond to market shifts as they happen. "Or instead of a marketing team waiting on an analyst to produce a report, they can simply ask, 'Which campaigns generated the highest ROI last month?' They can then drill down further, breaking down by region or identifying which audience segments converted best." Rich explains that a process that used to take days, can now be completed in a matter of minutes, adding: "Given the pace of modern businesses, this empowers decision-makers like never before and acts as a key strategic differentiator." Genie One helps employees work across fragmented company data Rich explains that, for most employees, the challenge is the spread of data across countless systems and applications. "Finding the right information often means switching between dashboards, documents, emails and collaboration tools before you can even start making a decision," he says. “Genie One changes that by giving employees a single place to interact with their organisation's information using plain natural language. Whether they're looking for an answer, updating a report or automating part of a workflow, they don't need to know where the data lives or which system to access first. “That has the potential to fundamentally change how people work. Instead of spending time hunting for information or relying on technical teams to surface it, employees can focus on making decisions and moving work forward.” How Genie One supports Databricks' goal of democratising data and AI Data democratisation means giving everyone in an organisation the ability to access data along with the tools and training necessary to understand it. Databricks has argued that the benefits of democratising data include breaking down data silos, removing bottlenecks, optimising data management and increasing data-driven decisions. “For me,” Rich says, "democratising data isn't just about making information easier to access; it's about giving more people the ability to turn ideas into action. Too often, the people who understand the business best still have to rely on technical teams to answer questions, build reports or test new ideas. That slows innovation down. “Genie One helps shift that balance by putting AI into the hands of more employees, enabling them to explore information, automate routine work and make better-informed decisions without needing deep technical expertise. “Importantly, that wider access doesn't come at the expense of governance. Businesses can empower more people to work with data while maintaining the controls, security and oversight needed to scale AI responsibly. That's what true democratisation looks like.” What needs to happen for agentic AI to become a mainstream workplace tool “I think there's still a tendency to focus on the AI itself, when the real challenge is everything underneath it,” Rich says. Rich argues that agentic AI is only as effective as the data, systems and governance that support it. He says if agents can't access live information or operate across different parts of the business, they'll never deliver the value organisations are hoping for. “The next phase of AI adoption is less about building smarter agents and more about modernising the underlying data architecture,” Rich says. “Businesses need a single, governed foundation where operational and analytical data work together, giving AI access to accurate, real-time information without introducing unnecessary complexity. “Poor foundations and weak governance are at the heart of why so many businesses struggle to move their agentic AI experiments beyond the pilot phase. Once organisations consistently recognise the importance of getting these foundations right, we'll see a surge in high-performing agentic deployments that deliver measurable, long-term ROI.” Databricks strategic funding at US$188bn. Not long after the DATA + AI Summit in San Francisco, news broke that Databricks had secured a valuation of US$188bn following its latest funding round. It signed a term sheet for the round, which it expects to close later this summer, led by its existing investor Coatue. The Wall Street Journal noted that the firm's US$188bn valuation represents a 40% increase from its valuation in December 2025, when Databricks raised funds at a US$134bn valuation. Ali Ghodsi, Co-Founder and CEO of Databricks, says: "Enterprises are moving from tokenmaxxing to valuemaxxing. They don't want to burn expensive tokens on the smartest model for every task – they want the best outcome per dollar. "That means having the freedom to choose the right AI for the job." The company says it will use the new capital to accelerate its AI strategy which covers: Unity AI Gateway, its multi-AI governance solution that helps enterprises govern and control costs of AI Lakebase, its serverless Postgres database built for AI agents Genie, Databricks' AI coworker that turns business data into trusted answers and actions Genie is the Databricks AI experience for users. It gives users a single place to ask data questions in natural language, explore AI/BI dashboards and run Databricks Apps. Rich Radley EMEA VP of Field Engineering

The company calls Genie One "the next evolution of Genie," helping marketing, finance, sales and more automate and orchestrate their work grounded in real business data. Rich Radley, its EMEA VP of Field Engineering, is well placed to lift the lid on Genie One, not to mention Databricks's various innovation in the field of AI. In his role, Rich works with organisations across Europe to help them turn advances in data and AI into measurable business outcomes. Before joining Databricks, he spent almost a decade at Google, helping build Google Cloud's business across the UK and Ireland and supporting organisations as they modernised their technology and data strategies. “What really drew me to Databricks was the opportunity ahead,” Rich explains. “It felt like the company was at a real turning point, with AI changing not only the technology organisations use, but also the conversations they're having in the boardroom. That's something I find really exciting. “My role is about helping customers connect the technology with the business outcome, while supporting my team to have more strategic conversations that show how data and AI can create long-term value.” “ Given the pace of modern businesses, this empowers decision makers like never before and acts as a key strategic differentiator. ” Rich Radley Rich Radley, EMEA VP of Field Engineering How Genie One is different from other AI assistants Rich argues that we've reached a point where the AI models themselves are incredibly capable. He says the real challenge now is giving them enough understanding of a business to produce outputs that people can genuinely rely on. “Without that,” he says, "even the most advanced assistants can deliver responses that sound plausible but miss the nuances of how an organisation actually operates.” "Genie One addresses this issue directly by being powered by Genie Ontology, a live context layer that continuously learns from your organisation’s data, metrics, systems and knowledge. Rather than simply interpreting prompts or individual documents, it understands the relationships between them, enabling it to deliver responses that reflect how the business actually works.” Rich explains that, with it, employees can spend less time searching for information or validating AI outputs, and more time making decisions and taking action. “More importantly,” he goes on, "it opens up data and AI to far more people across the organisation, removing some of the traditional dependency on technical teams while still operating within the right governance and security guardrails. “That's where I think businesses will see the biggest impact." “ Businesses can empower more people to work with data while maintaining the controls, security and oversight needed to scale AI responsibly. That's what true democratisation looks like. ” Rich Radley EMEA VP of Field Engineering Interesting use cases from non-technical teams Rich argues that the real power of Genie One is "putting trusted data into the hands of those that need it in seconds, fundamentally changing the speed at which decisions are made". He continues: "Imagine a sales leader meeting with the CEO. Instead of saying they'll come back with the numbers, they can instantly access the latest data insights on their mobile device, analyse information in real time, ask follow-up questions and respond to market shifts as they happen. "Or instead of a marketing team waiting on an analyst to produce a report, they can simply ask, 'Which campaigns generated the highest ROI last month?' They can then drill down further, breaking down by region or identifying which audience segments converted best." Rich explains that a process that used to take days, can now be completed in a matter of minutes, adding: "Given the pace of modern businesses, this empowers decision-makers like never before and acts as a key strategic differentiator." Genie One helps employees work across fragmented company data Rich explains that, for most employees, the challenge is the spread of data across countless systems and applications. "Finding the right information often means switching between dashboards, documents, emails and collaboration tools before you can even start making a decision," he says. “Genie One changes that by giving employees a single place to interact with their organisation's information using plain natural language. Whether they're looking for an answer, updating a report or automating part of a workflow, they don't need to know where the data lives or which system to access first. “That has the potential to fundamentally change how people work. Instead of spending time hunting for information or relying on technical teams to surface it, employees can focus on making decisions and moving work forward.” How Genie One supports Databricks' goal of democratising data and AI Data democratisation means giving everyone in an organisation the ability to access data along with the tools and training necessary to understand it. Databricks has argued that the benefits of democratising data include breaking down data silos, removing bottlenecks, optimising data management and increasing data-driven decisions. “For me,” Rich says, "democratising data isn't just about making information easier to access; it's about giving more people the ability to turn ideas into action. Too often, the people who understand the business best still have to rely on technical teams to answer questions, build reports or test new ideas. That slows innovation down. “Genie One helps shift that balance by putting AI into the hands of more employees, enabling them to explore information, automate routine work and make better-informed decisions without needing deep technical expertise. “Importantly, that wider access doesn't come at the expense of governance. Businesses can empower more people to work with data while maintaining the controls, security and oversight needed to scale AI responsibly. That's what true democratisation looks like.” What needs to happen for agentic AI to become a mainstream workplace tool “I think there's still a tendency to focus on the AI itself, when the real challenge is everything underneath it,” Rich says. Rich argues that agentic AI is only as effective as the data, systems and governance that support it. He says if agents can't access live information or operate across different parts of the business, they'll never deliver the value organisations are hoping for. “The next phase of AI adoption is less about building smarter agents and more about modernising the underlying data architecture,” Rich says. “Businesses need a single, governed foundation where operational and analytical data work together, giving AI access to accurate, real-time information without introducing unnecessary complexity. “Poor foundations and weak governance are at the heart of why so many businesses struggle to move their agentic AI experiments beyond the pilot phase. Once organisations consistently recognise the importance of getting these foundations right, we'll see a surge in high-performing agentic deployments that deliver measurable, long-term ROI.” Databricks strategic funding at US$188bn. Not long after the DATA + AI Summit in San Francisco, news broke that Databricks had secured a valuation of US$188bn following its latest funding round. It signed a term sheet for the round, which it expects to close later this summer, led by its existing investor Coatue. The Wall Street Journal noted that the firm's US$188bn valuation represents a 40% increase from its valuation in December 2025, when Databricks raised funds at a US$134bn valuation. Ali Ghodsi, Co-Founder and CEO of Databricks, says: "Enterprises are moving from tokenmaxxing to valuemaxxing. They don't want to burn expensive tokens on the smartest model for every task – they want the best outcome per dollar. "That means having the freedom to choose the right AI for the job." The company says it will use the new capital to accelerate its AI strategy which covers: Unity AI Gateway, its multi-AI governance solution that helps enterprises govern and control costs of AI Lakebase, its serverless Postgres database built for AI agents Genie, Databricks' AI coworker that turns business data into trusted answers and actions Genie is the Databricks AI experience for users. It gives users a single place to ask data questions in natural language, explore AI/BI dashboards and run Databricks Apps. Rich Radley EMEA VP of Field Engineering

articles.full_article_text: Since 2025, JAM Software has been transitioning most TreeSize editions to subscription models. Today, it sells perpetual licenses only for personal use, which include 12 months of updates, support, and “downloads of older versions, and your license,” plus the option to extend the support period. TreeSize currently has “no plans to discontinue the sale of perpetual licenses for TreeSize Personal,” product manager Hendrik Christ told Ars Technica. As perpetual-license maintenance periods expire, customers are discovering that extending support now generally requires subscribing to software they already own the right to use. On Reddit , a user shared an email informing them that support for their perpetual license ends in September, after which they will lose access to updates and support because those “are only available in the subscription.” Christ told Ars that considering the “current economic conditions,” the change was “necessary to keep developing and supporting TreeSize reliably over the long term.” One of the biggest criticisms is that JAM Software will not provide backup installation files or license keys to customers with unsupported licenses. TreeSize’s email urged the user to make backups. “Honestly, it feels quite low to strip paying customers of the ability to simply download the installer for a software version they already paid for,” the Reddit user said. But even before it sold TreeSize subscriptions, JAM Software didn’t permanently retain every installation file and key after a customer’s support period ended, Christ said. This is because “older software versions can contain known bugs or even security vulnerabilities,” he said, adding: Making these available for download indefinitely and without restriction is something we consider a risk to our customers, particularly in business environments. There’s also the technical and organizational overhead of maintaining and supporting old versions and their associated keys indefinitely. Although TreeSize says this is a longstanding policy, the backlash highlights the disconnect between what many people expect when buying a perpetual license and what they get when a software vendor shifts its business model toward subscriptions. “To make sure customers aren’t caught off guard, we proactively notify them by email, well before their maintenance ends, to back up their installation file and license key themselves. This is meant to ensure no one loses access to software they’ve already purchased,” Christ said. Should this be a subscription? Christ admitted that the change has been “frustrating for some customers.” When asked about online requests for refunds, Christ said, “since our customers do receive what was agreed, namely indefinite use of the software version they purchased, we don’t consider a refund to be warranted…” A free version of TreeSize exists, but it lacks some features, including the ability to search for duplicate files, deduplicate redundant files, and compare disk space usage over time. It is not for business use. TreeSize’s evolution illustrates the growing subscription economy, particularly the software industry’s fixation on recurring revenue. Over the past decade, software vendors have increasingly shifted to subscriptions in pursuit of more predictable revenue streams. In TreeSize’s case, JAM Software wanted to “continue offering our customers a relevant, well-maintained product over the long term,” Christ said. “The broader economic environment is more challenging today than it was a few years ago, and we feel that too as a software vendor,” he added. “To continue meeting our own standards and our responsibility to business customers who rely on high-quality software, we are placing greater emphasis on predictability in development and support. A subscription model gives us that predictability in a way one-time purchases do not.”

articles.full_article_text: Do you use your vehicle’s app to pre‑cool the cabin on a scorching day, confirm the doors are locked from bed, or have the car automatically call for help when the airbags go off? Savor those connected, cloud‑based conveniences while you can—the clock is already ticking on their obsolescence. In a few short years, you may be driving today’s vehicle without many of the features you currently enjoy. How we got hooked on the cloud “Connected services”—cloud-based and networked features that let a vehicle communicate with external systems to deliver apps, data, and remote functions to drivers and passengers—have been around since the 1990s, when GM introduced OnStar as an option. Those early systems were mostly voice‑centric, but they still depended on centralized back‑end systems. Modern versions, which are fully data-driven and cloud-hosted, use much more sophisticated over-the-air data links to allow a considerably better feature set. Today, virtually every volume brand offers some form of cloud-based telematics or a connected services stack. They can be deeply embedded, and most are fully integrated as the core of modern vehicle connectivity, supporting over-the-air (OTA) updates for the vehicle and app-based services for owners. As GM’s OnStar celebrates more than 30 years of service, a dozen others have joined, with each automaker branding its own unique services. HondaLink, Lexus Enform, FordPass, BMW ConnectedDrive, Volvo On Call, and Porsche Connect are just a few. Despite their catchy marketing names, the systems are all functionally similar—each offers a very comparable feature set. Basics include remote lock/start, vehicle status and maintenance updates, location and tracking, and emergency assistance. Additional premium features include in-vehicle Wi-Fi hotspots, cabin preconditioning, stolen-vehicle tracking services, and concierge owner services. Plenty of consumers have embraced the remote conveniences and demonstrated to automakers that they are more than willing to pay for them. After a bundled “free trial” following new vehicle delivery, manufacturers charge monthly fees or subscriptions for connected services. GM said that 40 percent of OnStar customers choose to renew their subscriptions after the introductory period expired. Why automakers love a connected car Of course, the OEMs get something out of it, too. Cloud-based services allow manufacturers to perform OTA software updates, eliminating the need to pay dealers for labor-intensive warranty repairs such as software-related safety recalls, bug fixes, and powertrain calibration errors. Instead of repairing one vehicle at a time, automakers can push updates to thousands of vehicles simultaneously. Plus, they can offer “product improvements” to owners, including UX changes, ADAS refinements, and new software versions for infotainment apps long after the start of production. Vehicles require unique hardware for OTA and connected services, of course. The basic components of original equipment (OE) hardware in most passenger vehicles include a telematics box (TCU) with a 3G/4G/5G modem, a SIM/eSIM, and antennas—these comprise the “smartphone” component. There’s also a main onboard computer with flash memory and a boot system to install the new hardware (programmed to revert to early code if something goes wrong so the car doesn’t “brick” itself). The TCU/main computer is tasked with sending signals over the vehicle’s internal wiring (CAN/Ethernet) to various ECUs, which are engineered to accept updates. For everyone’s peace of mind, robust security measures must be put in place to ensure that only genuine factory software can be installed and that hackers are locked out. Subscription costs aside, consumers are generally pleased with cloud-based services. Connectivity improves convenience, comfort, and safety, while OTA updates keep vehicles feeling fresh and up to date. Unfortunately, that honeymoon phase doesn’t last forever—over time, vehicle-cloud-based connected services are scaled back or, worse, shut off entirely. The day the signal dies There is no single event or element that triggers the end—it’s a combination of things. As vehicles age, OE on-board hardware becomes obsolete as cellular providers replace older technology and automakers stop investing in aging back-end stacks and features. Manufacturer contracts for connected services can also expire. Taken together, these factors mean that time ultimately kills cloud-based vehicle services. In 2022, many US cellular carriers, including AT&T, T‑Mobile/Sprint, and Verizon, shut down their 3G networks to create system capacity for upcoming 4G and 5G rollouts. When the 3G signal finally ceased, vehicles with the technology lost their connected cloud-based services (Porsche, Nissan, and Volkswagen were just a few of the automakers affected). Lexus owners felt this shift acutely. The company’s Enform connectivity, which relied on the 3G network and was fitted to nearly all 2010–2017 models, went dark overnight because the hardware simply wasn’t forward‑compatible. (Lexus refunded owners for paid time left, while opportunistic dealers suggested that frustrated owners upgrade to a new Lexus that supported current technology.) Last year, Acura announced that it would stop supporting vehicles with the older AcuraLink-backed stack and feature set, eliminating app-based remote access, service reminders, lock/unlock capabilities, “Find My Car,” and emergency call functions for many owners. The announcement itself was unremarkable, but many were stunned to learn that the technology was fitted to 2014–2022 models, including cars with current 4G hardware. Even though the vehicles and their modems could connect, Acura chose to stop supporting the old AcuraLink backend stack and feature set because the company determined it wasn’t worth it. Obsolescence was not an issue. (Acura provided prorated refunds to the relatively small number of customers still on paid plans but offered no retrofit path or migration for those vehicles that lost services.) In early 2022, BMW ended ConnectedDrive/BMW Assist services for vehicles equipped with 3G telematics. As the end date neared, owners were not permitted to renew their contracts. That February, when the official stop date arrived, all 3G services were terminated, even for those with vehicle connectivity that functioned perfectly. (BMW provided selected owners with other complimentary services; some vehicles with 4G-capable telematics were offered an upgrade at no charge, but many simply lost connectivity altogether.) Life after the shutdown When cloud-based connectivity goes away, it’s more of an inconvenience than a disaster. While remote conveniences and safety services end, they don’t serve an important role in the vehicle’s daily mechanical operation, meaning the powertrain, climate control, and accessories continue to work. But what if you use those cloud-based features and need an alternative once the existing system shuts off? Thankfully, there are a handful of possibilities, including software/OTA updates, hardware/TCU replacements, aftermarket telematics and OBD devices, and smartphone apps to keep vehicles connected to the cloud. Software/OTA updates are the easiest path to restore cloud services, but that assumes the vehicle has the proper hardware installed. Some 2017–2019 Genesis vehicles, including G80 and G90 models, used an SVLTE-type telematics system that could be upgraded with new software (the pure 3G-only units lost services when Verizon dropped its 3G network). Honda offered many customers free over-the-air software upgrades to 4G LTE in advance of AT&T’s cutoff. And GM brand owners, including those with Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC vehicles, were offered over-the-air software updates that preserved core OnStar services even after the first 3G network ceased. Nissan offered a $199 2G‑to‑3G TCU upgrade, which was partially subsidized by the manufacturer, for many 2011–2014 Leaf models but then offered the same upgrade to 2015 Leaf owners for free. BMW told i3 owners that no official technology upgrade was available, so owners took matters into their own hands and bought up-to-date 4G TCUs and paid to have them coded—this cost upward of $1,400 per vehicle. Although less integrated with the vehicle’s systems, aftermarket telematics and diagnostic-port (OBD) solutions offer limited cloud connectivity to fill the gap left by OE services when they’re phased out. Unfortunately, most are engineered for fleet services—creating app-based trip logs, GPS tracking, driving-style scoring, and basic OBD fault-code data for remote monitoring and data logging. They’re effective in this role, but they generally can’t duplicate OEM functions such as remote lock/engine start, automatic crash notification, or SOS features because they sit on the OBD port rather than on the carmaker’s proprietary telematics stack. While remote lock/engine start and climate control preconditioning typically aren’t part of the Apple CarPlay and Android Auto equation, most smartphones offer some sort of crash‑detection and SOS functions, reincorporating some of the important safety features lost with OEM cloud-based systems. Mobile phones also offer Wi-Fi via mobile hotspots, adding another useful feature. Phone-driven connectivity, with cloud services routed through CarPlay and Android Auto, has proven both dependable and virtually seamless for some drivers. A connected future with an expiration date Cloud-based vehicle connectivity is growing. While only about half of the vehicles on the road today utilize the technology, industry experts predict that 90–95 percent of new vehicles will be Internet‑connected by 2030. Most vehicles, even those on the assembly line today, still rely on embedded modem-based hardware. That means they’ll all eventually face the same obsolescence challenges. One proposed solution to the problem is modular software-defined architecture at the OE level, allowing consumers to physically swap hardware and upgrade software as technology advances. That welcome advancement would allow owners to upgrade their cloud-based connectivity and services rather than simply go dark.

HondaLink, Lexus Enform, FordPass, BMW ConnectedDrive, Volvo On Call, and Porsche Connect are just a few. Despite their catchy marketing names, the systems are all functionally similar—each offers a very comparable feature set. Basics include remote lock/start, vehicle status and maintenance updates, location and tracking, and emergency assistance. Additional premium features include in-vehicle Wi-Fi hotspots, cabin preconditioning, stolen-vehicle tracking services, and concierge owner services. Plenty of consumers have embraced the remote conveniences and demonstrated to automakers that they are more than willing to pay for them. GM said that 40 percent of OnStar customers choose to renew their subscriptions after the introductory period expired. articles.full_article_text: A recent examination of hundreds of mobile apps marketed toward US military personnel found more than one in eight contained software built by companies in China , Russia , or other foreign nations, raising fresh concerns that adversary governments could harvest data revealing where service members live, work, and deploy. According to researchers at Purdue University, the US Military Academy at West Point, and Florida International University , one popular app used by service members to rate living conditions on their own bases include code from Huawei, the Chinese telecom that US regulators flagged as a national security threat in 2020. Two others were built by Russian companies and incorporate the Russian ad service Yandex. The largely unregulated advertising industry that tracks Americans online treats civilians and service members mostly the same—unless there is profit in telling them apart —despite evidence that exposure can reveal troop deployments, unit movements, and the routines of personnel within intelligence facilities and hardened shelters where nuclear weapons are believed to be stored. WIRED investigations have previously shown location data harvested from ordinary apps tracing US service members to their homes, their children’s schools, and off-base establishments where troops are prohibited from being seen. Experts have warned the same data could aid foreign spies in identifying personnel with access to sensitive sites , map when a facility is least guarded, or surface other compromising details. The stakes are no longer hypothetical. In April, US Central Command acknowledged in a letter to Senator Ron Wyden that it had received multiple threat reports of adversaries exploiting commercial location data to target or surveil American personnel in the Middle East, where US forces remain locked in a standoff with the Iranian military over the Strait of Hormuz. Lawmakers called it the first official confirmation that troops in an active war zone were being hunted through the data-broker economy—a threat the Pentagon’s own contractors and researchers had warned about for nearly a decade. The new study takes a first look at one piece of that exposure: what actually sits inside the apps built and marketed specifically for the military. “We are grateful for the opportunity to bring greater attention to these issues,” says Joshua Shinkle, a Purdue University PhD researcher and the study’s lead author. “We hope the research helps military-affiliated personnel, developers, and platforms make more informed privacy decisions and encourages continued discussion with developers, platforms, and policymakers about how to address these gaps.” The researchers examined more than 220 such apps—from uniform guides and promotion-exam prep to banking and dating apps—pulled from the Google Play store and military subreddits. Nearly two-thirds—or 64 percent—contained third-party code, known as SDKs: prebuilt software components, typically used for analytics and advertising, that can also track user behavior, including their locations, and share that information with outside companies. Forty percent of the apps collected or shared more data than they disclosed in their Google or Apple store listings, the researchers found. The most common SDKs came from Google and Facebook, the two companies that dominate US digital advertising. But 76 turned up in all, including code traced back to China, Russia, Israel, India, Germany, and others. Roughly 7 percent of the apps carried third-party code from a nation considered adversarial by the Pentagon. Twelve of the apps contained HMS Core, a Huawei software kit that advertises the ability to map user locations, deliver ads, and store images and video. Several were built for state National Guard organizations. The researchers observed no data actually going to Huawei servers. But an SDK can be updated remotely at any time. Code that is dormant today can still be spyware tomorrow. In at least one case, noted by the study, the Huawei code arrived without the app’s developer’s knowledge, smuggled in as a dependency in a commercial notification tool. The researchers also surveyed 103 military-affiliated Americans—active-duty service members, reservists, veterans, DoD civilians, and their families—about the data practices they encountered on their own phones. More than 83 percent used at least one app engaging in data practices they said made them uncomfortable. On average, those participants used more than three such apps. Between 76 and 83 percent of participants said they were extremely uncomfortable with apps containing code from China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea—the four nations the Pentagon designates as cyber adversaries. But no user has a straightforward way to know which apps carry such code. Neither Google’s Play Store Data Safety section nor Apple’s App Store Privacy Labels disclose the country of origin of the software running inside an app. Participants reported being more comfortable with data collection when an app was branded for military use. Meanwhile, nearly two-thirds said they had received little or no institutional guidance on personal app use. Of those who had received some, nearly three-quarters called it inadequate. The Pentagon declined to comment. Asked to weigh potential mitigations, participants ranked in-phone warnings—alerts when foreign or unknown third-party code is present in an installed app—as both the most effective and the most likely for them to support. A federal law restricting data brokers from buying or selling data on military-affiliated personnel, independent audits of app privacy disclosures, and stricter bans on foreign code in military-marketed apps drew nearly identical support. This story originally appeared on wired.com .

In at least one case, noted by the study, the Huawei code arrived without the app’s developer’s knowledge, smuggled in as a dependency in a commercial notification tool. The researchers also surveyed 103 military-affiliated Americans—active-duty service members, reservists, veterans, DoD civilians, and their families—about the data practices they encountered on their own phones. More than 83 percent used at least one app engaging in data practices they said made them uncomfortable. On average, those participants used more than three such apps. Between 76 and 83 percent of participants said they were extremely uncomfortable with apps containing code from China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea—the four nations the Pentagon designates as cyber adversaries. But no user has a straightforward way to know which apps carry such code. Neither Google’s Play Store Data Safety section nor Apple’s App Store Privacy Labels disclose the country of origin of the software running inside an app. Participants reported being more comfortable with data collection when an app was branded for military use. Meanwhile, nearly two-thirds said they had received little or no institutional guidance on personal app use. Of those who had received some, nearly three-quarters called it inadequate. The Pentagon declined to comment. Asked to weigh potential mitigations, participants ranked in-phone warnings—alerts when foreign or unknown third-party code is present in an installed app—as both the most effective and the most likely for them to support. A federal law restricting data brokers from buying or selling data on military-affiliated personnel, independent audits of app privacy disclosures, and stricter bans on foreign code in military-marketed apps drew nearly identical support. This story originally appeared on wired.com .

articles.title: Stop Saying Kids Can’t Read
articles.fetched_title: Stop Saying Kids Can’t Read
articles.meta_description: Everyone is talking about the reading crisis. But inside the “Mississippi Miracle,” it’s all about comprehension.

article_images.alt: Stop Saying Kids Can’t Read
Stop Saying Kids Cant Read
Candace Hamberlin an eighthgrade English teacher at Jefferson County Middle School.
Hamberlin leading a session in her class of eighthgrade students.

Hamberlin leading a session in her class of eighthgrade students.

articles.full_article_text: Evidence of what’s at stake hangs all around Jefferson County Middle School, where Hamberlin is in her first year teaching eighth-grade English. Inside her classroom, a large piece of black polyester with clear pouches labeled “Data Wall” shows the current reading level of each student. The school hallways are lined with posters listing schoolwide scores on an earlier practice test. One prominently displays the grade Mississippi would assign their school if that practice test had been the real thing: 175 out of 700 points, an F. Jefferson County is one of the smallest in Mississippi; 6,800 people spread across 527 square miles along the Mississippi River. It’s also one of the poorest, with 32 percent of the population living below the poverty line. Fayette, where the only public elementary, middle, and high school are all based, is the only city in the county, home to about a dozen churches but not a single stoplight. The county is 13 percent white, but most of those families send their kids to private or parochial schools; 98 percent of the school district’s students are Black. Inside Hamberlin’s classroom, it’s time for test-prep drills. This period has 20 eighth graders enrolled, but only 10 are present; six have been pulled out for remedial work with a consultant the district has hired to boost test scores, and the remaining four are absent for unclear reasons. The students in the room each grab a Chromebook and log in, at speeds ranging from feet-dragging to actively resistant. They open the StudySync software program, which shows them each a series of questions tailored to their weaknesses. Their faces look like they’re being marched to the guillotine. Much of literacy instruction at Jefferson County Middle School now begins and ends with screens. In fact, Hamberlin doesn’t lecture at all on Wednesdays and Thursdays; students spend those class periods with StudySync and i-Ready, another adaptive software program, so each can focus where they need the most help. Their teacher can’t blame them for being sick of these exercises. The students’ lives, and hers, are dominated by the looming Mississippi Academic Assessment Program (MAAP), the set of annual standardized exams that measure their progress in language arts as well as science and math. Test prep is a year-round activity. Her students must learn how to decode the meaning of unfamiliar words, make inferences, identify the central idea of a passage, analyze tone and point of view. Every Friday brings a practice test. Before moving to eighth grade, Hamberlin logged 25 years as an elementary school teacher. Eighth grade appealed to her because it’s all about analyzing texts, not just consuming them. That’s her idea of a good time. She remembers reading the first chapter of the first Harry Potter book four times just to make sure she didn’t miss a single detail. As she talks a group of students through a reading passage by Sojourner Truth, her passion is palpable—for the material, but even more for the puzzle-solving that reading comprehension requires. “A lot of them think they’re studying the story,” she says afterward. “You’re not studying the story, that’s just the sprinkles on top. It’s what was she thinking, why did she say it, how did she convey her message?” Despite her clear talent and enthusiasm for teaching, though, Hamberlin has thus far failed to convince many of her students to care about reading. Earlier in the year, barely half of the eighth graders scored high enough to pass the all--important exam, and less than 15 percent are scoring “proficient.” If that F on the final schoolwide practice test had been the real thing, it would have been disastrous; Mississippi’s letter grading system comes with steep real-world consequences. Low-performing schools can face state monitoring, while their funding is more likely to come with “accountability” strings attached. State law allows students to attend out-of-district charter schools only when their home district is failing, so low scores can result in a decrease in funding because fewer students are enrolled. Superintendents and principals know that their jobs are tied to increasing scores or at least not allowing them to drop. Across the country, reading performance has slid for 14 years, and the problem is most extreme in middle and high school. Even in Mississippi, where the improvement in elementary school test scores has become the stuff of legend, older students are struggling. No one can quite agree on why reading scores have dropped so far. And that’s just what the tests measure. Hamberlin’s true fears are more existential. Hamberlin wants her students to pass the exam, but what she really wants is to build them into readers; adults who can interpret a complex set of instructions, power through a confusing block of text, and—hopefully, maybe, at least a few—actually read books. “It’s as simple as understanding a conversation. How many times have you talked to someone and you’re talking about two different things?” she says. “All those skills from reading just transfer to life completely.” Plenty of her students are smart and capable, but she’s never encountered a group less interested in reading. And neither she nor anyone else seems to have any idea how to fix it. Citing a decline in SAT scores over the preceding two decades, A Nation at Risk’s authors framed their concerns in geo-political terms, warning that countries like Japan and South Korea were poised to overtake the US in global economic rankings if American students didn’t make significant gains. Their language was hyperbolic to the point of scare--mongering: “If an unfriendly foreign power had attempted to impose on America the mediocre educational performance that exists today, we might well have viewed it as an act of war,” the introduction read. “As it stands, we have allowed this to happen to ourselves.” One bullet point reported that one--quarter of Navy recruits could not read at a ninth-grade level, “the minimum needed simply to understand written safety instructions. Without remedial work they cannot even begin, much less complete, the sophisticated training essential in much of the modern military.” In the four decades since, at least one of the authors of A Nation at Risk has backed away from its findings, saying the commission cherry-picked the data that best served their preexisting thesis that American schools were failing. They did accomplish their goals, though: The report called for the adoption of “more rigorous and measurable standards” in schools, and throughout the ’90s, states designed their own standardized tests to be administered across all school districts. The march toward high-stakes testing crescendoed with President George W. Bush’s signature education reform program, No Child Left Behind, signed into law in 2002, which required standards-based exams in reading and math for every public school student in the country. Schools that didn’t meet standards risked state takeovers. Detractors have long questioned the validity of test scores, pointing to built-in bias among other issues. Even so, state testing has become the most important measure of reading skills by a huge margin. NAEP reading scores did rise, modestly, in the first part of the 21st century (at least among elementary and middle schoolers; high school scores stayed largely flat). Scores for 13-year-olds moved from 259 to 263 on a 500-point scale between 1999 and 2012; 9-year-olds improved from 212 to 221. The narrative that American schools were failing faded from conventional wisdom. Then reading performance began to drop again. Among 13-year-olds, scores fell to 260 by 2020, nearly erasing the previous gains. The pandemic made things worse. By 2025, 13-year-old scores had plunged to 256, just a point above where they were in 1971. (Math scores have seen a similar decline.) Scores ticked up slightly among 9-year-olds in 2026 and remained at the prior year’s levels among 13-year-olds. One-third of 13-year-olds score “below basic” on standardized reading tests, meaning they can’t identify the main idea in a passage. Panic roared back. Secretary of education Linda McMahon said the national results in 2024 “confirm a devastating trend”; The Atlantic said the country was “sliding toward illiteracy”; New York magazine labeled the drift “The Big Fail.” Much of the uproar sounded straight out of A Nation at Risk: “If policy-makers and education leaders fail to act now, students—and employers—will feel the impact of declining skills and knowledge gaps as the global workforce becomes more and more competitive,” the chair of the National Assessment Governing Board said in a press release. Everyone had a pet theory as to what had gone wrong: smartphones, bad teachers, bad textbooks, lazy students, lazy families. A 2022 podcast called Sold a Story, about the problematic rise of the “balanced literacy” teaching method in elementary schools, revealed a pedagogical issue in the US: Many teachers were, basically, asking kids to guess at sentences instead of making them sound the words out. As in-school apps began incorporating generative artificial intelligence, the fears intensified. Many schools now introduce AI starting in kindergarten, saying kids have to be prepared for a future in which it’s the norm. Maybe using AI tools will improve standardized test scores; it’s too early to tell. But it’s more difficult to believe those tools will improve literacy in the truer sense, that students will fully develop the cognitive skills to do the work themselves when they don’t have to. “There’s no question that the engagement’s gone,” says Kevin Smith, an education scholar who co-leads the Adolescent Literacy Alliance at Florida State University’s Florida Center for Reading Research. “I’m not saying they’re not reading, but they’re not reading books for the love of books. They’re reading probably more than they ever have, but it’s snippets.” Earlier this year, a team of researchers from Harvard, Stanford, and Dartmouth declared the US was in “a learning recession.” And suddenly, everyone was looking to Mississippi for the answers. LaTasha Glass, 30, is in her first year teaching in Fayette after six years in her hometown of Natchez, a bigger, more touristy town on the river. With a daughter in fifth grade at Jefferson County Elementary, she brings a maternal air to class, providing warm encouragement and tough-love coaching in equal measure. She’s dressed for a day on her feet, in a lavender short-sleeved shirt over black stretchy pants and outdoorsy sandals, but her hair is stylishly braided, and silver bangles clink on her wrist. Glass started her career teaching second grade, but a previous principal convinced her she had what it took to get third graders over the test hurdle. That’s not an easy sell for many teachers; Jefferson County Elementary principal Shameka Woods says she’s asked the school district to pay third-grade teachers more because they’re so hard to hire. “No one wants to teach third grade!” Woods says. Glass pipes up, mostly joking but not entirely: “I asked her yesterday to put me back in second grade!” Her first-block class makes clear why Glass is so valuable in the highest-stakes teaching role. From the time the bell rings, she has her students’ complete attention. The moment she senses she’s at risk of losing even a couple of them, she shouts out one of her bespoke call-and-response mantras that immediately brings them back: Mac and cheese? Everybody freeze! Class class? Ms. Glass! Hocus pocus? Everybody focus! Ready set? You bet! Today’s lesson is about r-controlled vowels, a phonics concept about how the vowel sound in words like car or bird changes because of the r that follows it. Glass breaks down a few words on the smart whiteboard at the front of the classroom, but with plenty of pauses to ask for student contributions. To make things more fun, she plays a YouTube video from an education creator known as Mrs. Siravo, a parody of the Jonas Brothers song “Sucker” listing words shaped by this kind of “bossy r.” Then it’s time for students to take turns coming to the board and diagramming their own words. “Circus,” a girl in a tie-dye fleece sweatshirt suggests, then writes it on the board as “curcus.” Glass lets the misspelling stand for the moment. The first task is to figure out the number of sounds in the word. Those who didn’t learn reading through phonics tend to assume the answer is two, but sounds are different from syllables. The actual answer is five: soft c, the growl of the r-controlled first vowel, hard c, “uh,” then s. The girl puts five dots under the word, and the whole class claps out the sounds. Now Glass returns to the spelling issue. Other r-controlled vowels can make that growling sound too, she reminds them. It must be an i, several students shout out. Their teacher grins, thrilled by their ability to sleuth out the correct answer. She knows the test weighs on these 8- and 9-year-olds. She tries to praise them frequently, and makes corrections in a supportive way. “They have anxiety,” she says. “I let them know how much pressure it is, but I try to alleviate some of the pressure. When they make a mistake, I make sure they learn from it.” With just a couple weeks until the test, she’s feeling confident in her students: Only five of the 40 scored below a passing mark on the final benchmark exam. This is what the “Mississippi Miracle” looks like in the classroom. In 2013, Mississippi ranked 49th out of 50 on the federally mandated NAEP tests, confirming the conventional wisdom about how poor, Republican-dominated states have weaker education systems than wealthier, more Democratic ones. But starting in 2015—the test is given every two years—the poorest state in the country began a steady climb through the ranks of fourth-grade scores. In just two years, the state’s reading performance jumped five points, then another five points four years after that. Scores dipped during the pandemic, but by a smaller margin than in many other states. By 2024, 11 years after coming in second-to-last, Mississippi ranked ninth in the country in fourth-grade reading. The legend of the “miracle” began to take hold. Jefferson County’s growth curve was even steeper. In 2013, the elementary school was among the worst performers in its underperforming state, earning an F rating. In 2022, just 43 percent of fourth graders passed the MAAP test. In 2025, 78 percent did, a 35-point jump in three years. Superintendent Adrian Hammitte, who’s in his seventh year as superintendent and his 16th in the district, was hoping for a 90 percent pass rate for third graders this year; preliminary data shows they landed in the mid-80s. “We want 100 percent,” he says, smiling, “but realistically, we’re shooting for 90.” Most of these theories collapse under scrutiny. There is zero evidence that Mississippi’s improved reading scores are the result of widespread fraud. And simply preventing the worst readers from taking the fourth-grade test doesn’t explain the dramatic jumps in Jefferson County, where Hammitte says not a single third grader was held back in 2024 or 2025. So why have elementary school reading scores jumped dramatically in places like Jefferson County, one of the poorest places in the poorest state in the country, at the same time national averages are plummeting? Hammitte believes the third-grade “reading gate” is in fact key to his district’s success—but not because it removes the weakest readers from the pool of fourth-grade test takers. Rather, he argues that third graders pass the test because their families see no choice but to pass; no one wants their child to be held back. Students who pass the third-grade state test are likely to repeat their success in fourth grade. “There’s so much pressure and so much emphasis on trying to get every child to pass the test,” he says, “not only because we know the state is going to report on it, but also because we know that if they don’t pass, they’re going to be retained.” The reading gate is part of a broader array of accountability mechanisms, including letter grades for each district and school, that trace their origins to the No Child Left Behind era and that have been controversial among many progressive education advocates because they can punish students and schools without solving underlying structural inequalities. They can also lead to higher stress, lower morale, and more turnover among teachers. In Mississippi and many other states, the entire year’s curriculum is determined by what’s on the test. “Reading” doesn’t mean books, but exercises like the ones Glass’ class does every morning, each tailored to a specific skill measured by the MAAP exam. Glass doesn’t design these lessons herself. As part of a move toward “high--quality instructional materials,” Mississippi strongly recommends that districts choose from a list of state-approved curricula, all tailored toward concepts on the spring exam. Those materials are based on scientific research into how children’s brains learn to read—not as an organic development, the belief that underpinned the “whole language” philosophy popular in the 1980s and ’90s, but through the building blocks of letters and sounds that make up phonics. To eliminate variability, Jefferson County classes use identical lesson plans; teachers can’t write their own material based on their students’ interests (or their own). Glass can’t just read from the script; the unplanned “curcus” conversation shows why even the best material still requires a teacher who can adapt on the fly. But as Glass walks through the concept of r-controlled vowels, the other third-grade language arts teacher down the hall is reading the exact same examples. The reading gate and uniform teaching materials have gotten the most attention from those who believe Mississippi should be a model for the rest of the country. But sitting in on Glass’ class suggests that another part of the Literacy-Based Promotion Act may in fact be the most important key to improving reading performance. Aside from its accountability measures, the law also provided $9.5 million in annual funding for literacy coaches and teacher training. (Today it’s up to $15 million a year.) Michelle Nowell, the associate state superintendent overseeing curriculum and instruction, runs a team of 57 coaches focusing on kindergarten through third grade, with 22 more due to be hired before the next school year. Those coaches float among districts, focusing on those that need the most improvement. “If you said, ‘Why do you think y’all been so successful in K-3?’ I would say it’s boots on the ground with our literacy coaches,” Nowell says. “We are not evaluative, we’re not punitive. We build relationships, and we’re there to help.” Many districts, including Jefferson County, have carved out money for their own coaches. Last fall, Hammitte hired fourth-grade teacher Timothy Queen as the elementary school’s instructional coach. Queen, who’s also a cheerleading coach at nearby Alcorn State University, is a ball of energy and enthusiasm, constantly doling out hugs and fist bumps to students as his long braid bounces against his shoulders. His job is to train his colleagues, not work with students, but he can end up functioning as a second teacher during a given lesson. With the all-important test approaching, both Queen and principal Shameka Woods are focusing much of their energy on third-grade classes. The result is that, at least during the spring, Glass is rarely leading her classroom alone. When she breaks her 20-ish students into small groups, she can check on half of them while Queen or Woods handles the rest. When a boy starts nodding off, Queen escorts him into the hallway to splash water on his face. As Glass talks through which letter combinations form which sounds, Queen jumps in to guide a brief discussion of the vowel sound in “cycle.” “What does that second letter sound like?” he asks, prompting one talkative boy to suggest “i.” “What’s the other letter” that makes an “i” sound, Queen responds. “Y!” the kids yell triumphantly. As a result, third-grade class periods are a stream of engaging activities: diagramming sounds on the board, watching a YouTube song, calling out answers, doing call-and-response. Hamberlin’s eighth graders sit quietly and read long passages about topics ranging from how elephants use their trunks to 19th-century history. The Mississippi Miracle suggests the state may have cracked the code of how to teach basic literacy. The conundrum is that even there, success peters out when it comes to translating words into conceptual thinking. “Sometimes students are distracted by the format of the test, and so they get the practice test and they read the paragraph and answer the questions,” says Laurie Lee, who co-leads the Adolescent Literacy Alliance, which ran a pilot training program for fourth- through eighth-grade teachers in three Mississippi school districts this school year. “But ultimately what will help is if the kids can actually read the texts and comprehend.” Nationwide, middle-school reading scores began their decline a couple of years before elementary-school scores, creating a downward trend line that has lasted nearly 15 years. Eighth-grade performance on the National Assessment of Educational Progress is now one point shy of an all-time low. The number of eighth graders scoring “below basic” is the highest ever recorded. Among Mississippi eighth graders, the drop in reading scores began a few years after the nation as a whole, but the curve was even steeper, losing three points between 2017 and 2022 and remaining flat in 2024. Theoretically, a class of third graders who excel on the reading standardized test would turn into a class of eighth graders who not only excel on that test but also apply those skills to the world around them, and then into a group of adults who are literate in a way that has nothing to do with tests at all. That’s not happening. A 2022 evaluation of adult literacy found that 28 percent of Americans cannot reliably compare and contrast information, paraphrase, or make basic inferences. Six years earlier, that number was 19 percent. Though the biggest drop was among adults who didn’t graduate from high school, even those with some amount of higher education got worse at reading. A 2023 National Endowment for the Arts survey, meanwhile, found that less than half of adults had read a book in the past year. Experts worry these trends stem from habits that started earlier in their lives. In conversations with teachers and literacy experts, nearly everyone diagnoses the problem as one of attention span, not intelligence. “It’s really just about stamina,” Hamberlin says. “They have five to six passages. Some of them are informational, some of them are literature. And at a certain point they just don’t want to read anymore.” Students stop reading when they hit a word they don’t know, but they need to know how to decode unfamiliar words for the test as well as for the world. They lose focus if the subject doesn’t interest them, but they’ll encounter passages on all sorts of topics both on the test and in life. “A lot of people don’t engage with lengthy text, and that’s a muscle like you build working out,” says Kevin Smith, Lee’s codirector. “I don’t know if a lot of our kids have built the muscle to read longer texts.” The prime suspect is smartphones. A 2022 paper in the journal Developmental Neuropsychology synthesizing 11 studies found that 10 of them had identified a correlation between the amount of children’s screen time and their attention spans. Teens’ favorite apps seem to make the problems worse: Scrolling TikTok, which 61 percent of American teenagers do every day and one in five do “almost constantly,” means flicking away from a video the millisecond it becomes uninteresting. The more recent rise of generative AI, meanwhile, means never needing to struggle to understand a concept. You can’t change the reading passage on a standardized test no matter how boring it is. You can’t ChatGPT your way to the answer. Hamberlin’s eighth graders aren’t using AI on their reading assignments. But they seem to treat reading passages like they’re TikTok. Sick of reading about a long-dead abolitionist? Make a wisecrack to a classmate, fiddle with your pencil, ask to go to the bathroom—anything but powering through the reading. Teachers like to talk about “productive struggle,” the idea of grappling with a concept you don’t understand rather than either giving up or asking a bot to solve it for you. Students already seemed to be losing that instinct before the rise of AI. Now there’s even less reason to do the work. Screen time and social media don’t explain everything: The performance slide has affected some groups of students more than others, even though almost everyone has a smartphone. On some level, it doesn’t even matter how big of a problem they are, since kids aren’t going to stop using them. The thornier question for teachers and education officials is what can be done to improve reading scores in the world in which we live. Conservative education reformers argue that America’s education system has strayed too far from No Child Left Behind, that focusing on equity and moving away from high-stakes testing as part of efforts not to punish students for being racial minorities or low-income—both of which are correlated with lower reading performance—means districts are no longer maintaining high standards. Mississippi is as committed as ever to high-stakes testing, but the stakes are higher in third grade than in eighth. Under this theory, one solution would be a requirement that students pass the standardized test at the end of every grade before moving to the next. The research, though, is mixed at best about whether attaching harsher consequences to standardized tests actually results in better performance. And the decline in American reading goes deeper than the ability to pass a standardized test. Just 16 percent of Americans read for fun, according to a 2023 study, down from 28 percent in 2004. Only 41 percent of children under 4 are frequently read to, down 23 points since 2012. “I think there’s an important distinction between whether students are able to read and whether they’re willing to read,” says Jonathan Becker, a scholar of education policy at Virginia Commonwealth University. “If we want our students to be able to answer questions about a short reading passage, we’re going to have them read lots of short reading passages. There’s no real incentive on the tests or in a lot of the standards to have kids read whole books.” Mississippi’s definition of “passing” is counterintuitive. A student who passes MAAP is “approaching or at the level of difficulty, complexity, or fluency specified by the grade-level content standards.” In other words, they might not actually be on grade level. Students who show “solid academic performance and mastery” of skills at their grade level are scored “proficient.” Fifty-nine percent of Jefferson County third graders were proficient in reading last year, compared to just 24 percent of eighth graders. Even in Mississippi, the home of the most discussed miracle in contemporary education, teenagers are falling behind. In April, the Mississippi legislature approved pay raises for all teachers, plus an extra $9 million to hire literacy coaches specifically focused on fourth through eighth grades. The hope is that expanding the Florida literacy scholars’ pilot program will give teachers across the state better tools for teaching reading, and add another adult in the classroom at least some of the time. Literacy scholars agree that teaching reading across subjects is key. The ideal method of teaching students to read—rather than just passing reading tests—they say, is assigning them texts on subjects they’re interested in, whether that’s astronomy or the NFL. “I struggle to read things that are not interesting to me,” Becker says. “I do wonder how often we’re giving kids the option to read things that are interesting to them, so that maybe they can develop more stamina.” Hamberlin’s eighth-grade students read what’s assigned by their state- approved instructional materials; whether they’re interested is beside the point. They don’t even read books for class; there’s no time if they’re going to get through the whole MAAP curriculum. America’s fervor for standardized tests is fundamental to its education policy. If schools like this one can extend the Mississippi Miracle to middle school, if America is going to pull itself out of this standardized test score slump, it will happen through skill drills, not students losing themselves in novels. “Human flourishing is not as easily measurable as student achievement,” Becker says. “It’s harder for people to commit to things that aren’t measurable, that aren’t tangible, that we can’t really document.” This year, for the first time in her career, Hamberlin can’t think of a single student across her five periods who reads for fun, who considers her class anything beyond an ordeal to be survived. Even her strongest readers don’t particularly like doing it. “Usually in the classroom, somebody always has a book,” she says. “I don’t have any of them that has a book.” Adding a reading gate at the end of eighth grade might make more of them pass the test, she thinks, but it certainly wouldn’t make any of them read books. As Hamberlin works out her thoughts aloud, she notices a boy with close-cropped hair in a black Nike zip-up hoodie and black Air Jordans listening in. He’s supposed to be reading the assigned passage, but he’s gotten distracted a third of the way through. “You want to add anything about reading class and what kinds of things we do?” Hamberlin asks him. The boy shrugs his skinny shoulders. “It’s really boring,” he says, then turns back to Sojourner Truth. Let us know what you think about this article. Submit a letter to the editor at mail@wired.com.

One prominently displays the grade Mississippi would assign their school if that practice test had been the real thing: 175 out of 700 points, an F. It’s also one of the poorest, with 32 percent of the population living below the poverty line. Fayette, where the only public elementary, middle, and high school are all based, is the only city in the county, home to about a dozen churches but not a single stoplight. The county is 13 percent white, but most of those families send their kids to private or parochial schools; 98 percent of the school district’s students are Black. Inside Hamberlin’s classroom, it’s time for test-prep drills. This period has 20 eighth graders enrolled, but only 10 are present; six have been pulled out for remedial work with a consultant the district has hired to boost test scores, and the remaining four are absent for unclear reasons. The students in the room each grab a Chromebook and log in, at speeds ranging from feet-dragging to actively resistant. They open the StudySync software program, which shows them each a series of questions tailored to their weaknesses. Their faces look like they’re being marched to the guillotine. Much of literacy instruction at Jefferson County Middle School now begins and ends with screens. In fact, Hamberlin doesn’t lecture at all on Wednesdays and Thursdays; students spend those class periods with StudySync and i-Ready, another adaptive software program, so each can focus where they need the most help. Their teacher can’t blame them for being sick of these exercises. The students’ lives, and hers, are dominated by the looming Mississippi Academic Assessment Program (MAAP), the set of annual standardized exams that measure their progress in language arts as well as science and math. Test prep is a year-round activity. Her students must learn how to decode the meaning of unfamiliar words, make inferences, identify the central idea of a passage, analyze tone and point of view. Every Friday brings a practice test. Before moving to eighth grade, Hamberlin logged 25 years as an elementary school teacher. Eighth grade appealed to her because it’s all about analyzing texts, not just consuming them. That’s her idea of a good time. She remembers reading the first chapter of the first Harry Potter book four times just to make sure she didn’t miss a single detail. As she talks a group of students through a reading passage by Sojourner Truth, her passion is palpable—for the material, but even more for the puzzle-solving that reading comprehension requires. “A lot of them think they’re studying the story,” she says afterward. “You’re not studying the story, that’s just the sprinkles on top. It’s what was she thinking, why did she say it, how did she convey her message?” Despite her clear talent and enthusiasm for teaching, though, Hamberlin has thus far failed to convince many of her students to care about reading. Earlier in the year, barely half of the eighth graders scored high enough to pass the all--important exam, and less than 15 percent are scoring “proficient.” If that F on the final schoolwide practice test had been the real thing, it would have been disastrous; Mississippi’s letter grading system comes with steep real-world consequences. How many times have you talked to someone and you’re talking about two different things?” she says. “All those skills from reading just transfer to life completely.” Plenty of her students are smart and capable, but she’s never encountered a group less interested in reading. And neither she nor anyone else seems to have any idea how to fix it. Citing a decline in SAT scores over the preceding two decades, A Nation at Risk’s authors framed their concerns in geo-political terms, warning that countries like Japan and South Korea were poised to overtake the US in global economic rankings if American students didn’t make significant gains. They did accomplish their goals, though: The report called for the adoption of “more rigorous and measurable standards” in schools, and throughout the ’90s, states designed their own standardized tests to be administered across all school districts. The march toward high-stakes testing crescendoed with President George W. Bush’s signature education reform program, No Child Left Behind, signed into law in 2002, which required standards-based exams in reading and math for every public school student in the country. Schools that didn’t meet standards risked state takeovers. Detractors have long questioned the validity of test scores, pointing to built-in bias among other issues. Even so, state testing has become the most important measure of reading skills by a huge margin. Glass started her career teaching second grade, but a previous principal convinced her she had what it took to get third graders over the test hurdle. The moment she senses she’s at risk of losing even a couple of them, she shouts out one of her bespoke call-and-response mantras that immediately brings them back: Mac and cheese? Everybody freeze! There is zero evidence that Mississippi’s improved reading scores are the result of widespread fraud. And simply preventing the worst readers from taking the fourth-grade test doesn’t explain the dramatic jumps in Jefferson County, where Hammitte says not a single third grader was held back in 2024 or 2025. So why have elementary school reading scores jumped dramatically in places like Jefferson County, one of the poorest places in the poorest state in the country, at the same time national averages are plummeting? Hammitte believes the third-grade “reading gate” is in fact key to his district’s success—but not because it removes the weakest readers from the pool of fourth-grade test takers. Rather, he argues that third graders pass the test because their families see no choice but to pass; no one wants their child to be held back. Students who pass the third-grade state test are likely to repeat their success in fourth grade. “There’s so much pressure and so much emphasis on trying to get every child to pass the test,” he says, “not only because we know the state is going to report on it, but also because we know that if they don’t pass, they’re going to be retained.” The reading gate is part of a broader array of accountability mechanisms, including letter grades for each district and school, that trace their origins to the No Child Left Behind era and that have been controversial among many progressive education advocates because they can punish students and schools without solving underlying structural inequalities. They can also lead to higher stress, lower morale, and more turnover among teachers. As part of a move toward “high--quality instructional materials,” Mississippi strongly recommends that districts choose from a list of state-approved curricula, all tailored toward concepts on the spring exam. Those materials are based on scientific research into how children’s brains learn to read—not as an organic development, the belief that underpinned the “whole language” philosophy popular in the 1980s and ’90s, but through the building blocks of letters and sounds that make up phonics. Glass can’t just read from the script; the unplanned “curcus” conversation shows why even the best material still requires a teacher who can adapt on the fly. But as Glass walks through the concept of r-controlled vowels, the other third-grade language arts teacher down the hall is reading the exact same examples. Michelle Nowell, the associate state superintendent overseeing curriculum and instruction, runs a team of 57 coaches focusing on kindergarten through third grade, with 22 more due to be hired before the next school year. Those coaches float among districts, focusing on those that need the most improvement. “If you said, ‘Why do you think y’all been so successful in K-3?’ I would say it’s boots on the ground with our literacy coaches,” Nowell says. “We are not evaluative, we’re not punitive. We build relationships, and we’re there to help.” Many districts, including Jefferson County, have carved out money for their own coaches. Queen, who’s also a cheerleading coach at nearby Alcorn State University, is a ball of energy and enthusiasm, constantly doling out hugs and fist bumps to students as his long braid bounces against his shoulders. His job is to train his colleagues, not work with students, but he can end up functioning as a second teacher during a given lesson.
